analysis.one_liner: Requires citizen commissions, not legislators, to draw congressional maps and bans mid-decade redistricting.
analysis.headline: The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, but it never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have taken the drawing of congressional districts away from state legislators and given it to a 15-member citizen commission in each state, with rules requiring maps that do not unduly favor either political party. It would have banned states from redrawing their maps again before the next census unless a court ordered it. States that already used qualifying independent commissions, plus Iowa, would have been exempt. If a state's commission process broke down, a three-judge federal court would draw the map instead [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced by the Senate Majority Leader in August 2021, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, where it sat without any further action until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters whose ballots currently count for less because legislative-drawn maps are engineered to be safe for one party. The bill also would have let ordinary citizens apply to serve on the map-drawing commissions, given them a private right to sue states that did not comply, and required public hearings, published data, and online access to every draft map [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Redistricting would be done by an independent 15-member citizen commission, chosen through a public application process, rather than by the state legislators whose own seats the maps affect [S2][S3].
Maps could not unduly favor or disfavor any political party, with quantitative tests for partisan bias and a public written evaluation of each plan against accepted fairness measures [S2][S3].
States could not redraw congressional maps between censuses unless a court required it, stopping the practice of parties rewriting maps mid-decade when the political winds shift [S2][S3].
Any citizen aggrieved by a state's failure to comply could sue, with expedited three-judge court review and direct appeal to the Supreme Court [S3].
The federal Election Assistance Commission would fund the process at $150,000 per congressional seat, so states would not bear the cost [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent House members and state legislators of both parties, who would lose the power to draw the districts they run in and the safe seats that often come with it. The federal treasury would fund state commissions through appropriations [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill rests on Congress's power over congressional elections and would override the legislatures of most states, which have traditionally drawn congressional maps; that shift would almost certainly face legal challenge, and the bill's own text states its claimed constitutional authority [S3].
Its Title V would have applied these rules retroactively to redistricting already underway after the 2020 census, upending maps states were drawing in 2021 while the process was in motion [S3].

The commission process is elaborate: if a state's legislative-appointed committee rejects three successive candidate pools, or the commission misses its deadline, a three-judge federal court simply draws the map, substituting one unelected body for another [S2][S3].
The ban on mid-decade redistricting would lock in each decade's maps even if population shifts or legal rulings make them stale, with redrawing permitted only on court order [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is real: map drawing moves from the people who benefit from gerrymandered maps to citizen commissions with open processes, enforceable fairness standards, and funding from Washington rather than the states. The costs are mostly transition risk — constitutional challenge to federal control of redistricting, the complexity of the commission machinery, and a court fallback that is not clearly more accountable than what it replaces. The strongest good-faith objection is that a federal mandate overriding every state's process is a heavy-handed remedy; the strongest fact in its favor is that the current process is drawn by the people whose seats are at stake.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by the Senate Majority Leader, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but it never got a cosponsor, a hearing, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Charles Schumer, the Senate Majority Leader, introduced the bill on August 6, 2021; it was read a first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar [S5].
The next day, August 7, 2021, it was read a second time and placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 119 [S3][S5].
That placement on the calendar is the last action of any kind: no committee took it up, no hearing was held, and no vote occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
Not a single senator, including members of Schumer's own party, signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

The CRS summary describes the bill's core: redistricting by independent state commission or, failing that, a three-judge federal court, a ban on favoring a party, and a prohibition on mid-decade redistricting [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and state legislators of both parties, who kept the power to draw the districts they run in. Because the bill died without a vote, every safe seat drawn by a partisan legislature for the 2022 elections remained in place.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, and had it read twice and placed on the Senate calendar as Calendar No. 119; it never received further floor action

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Did not cosponsor the bill at any point during the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split can be measured; the bill's only recorded support was its Democratic sponsor, and it drew zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.industry: Incumbent members of the House of Representatives
industries.note: The bill removes the power of sitting representatives' allies in state legislatures to draw the districts representatives run in, threatening the safe seats many hold today. Its interest in the bill runs against voters' interest in competitive, fairly drawn districts [S2][S3].

industries.industry: State legislators and state party organizations
industries.note: Most states would lose the map-drawing power that lets legislative majorities entrench themselves for a decade. The bill exempts only states whose existing commissions already meet its standards, plus Iowa [S3].
